headline: La Trobe Financial deploying $1.5bn per month into Australian residential and commercial mortgages, describing the strategy as domestic private credit
reasoning: Chris Andrews notes that La Trobe's existing Australian portfolios are performing very well, with roughly $1.5 billion per month being deployed into residential and commercial mortgages. He observes that what is now labelled 'private credit' is essentially the same asset class La Trobe has operated in for decades. He is comfortable with the exposure and dismisses concern about label-driven categorisation, emphasising the importance of focusing on underlying portfolio fundamentals.
quote: We in terms of our existing portfolios, Andrew, they're performing really well. So we're deploying about 1.5 billion a month into, you know, residential and commercial mortgages here in Australia. These days, people call that private credit. Ten years ago no one was calling a private credit. So, you know, in terms of that exposure, we're very comfortable with that.
episode_title: $25bn milestone: Why income is back in vogue

headline: Ageing Australian population driving structural demand for stable income investments, with La Trobe seeing its fastest ever growth as retirees seek reliable returns
reasoning: Andrews observes that more and more investors are moving into or approaching retirement, and as demographics age, there is growing structural demand for consistent, stable, reliable income sources. La Trobe has been providing this for decades and is now seeing its fastest ever growth as a result. He expects consistent inflows to continue and plans to leverage scale advantages — including access to high quality deal flow, broader liquidity management, and technology investment — to benefit investors further.
quote: More and more investors are moving into that retirement space. Uh, Andrew, they're they're approaching retirement. They're in retirement. We all know Australia's population, like the rest of the world, is getting older on average over time. And as investors age, as investors approach retirement, they need consistent capital, stable, reliable type income sources. So we've been producing that for many decades. And what we're seeing now is we're growing faster than we've ever grown before. So it is it is a time where we're expecting to see consistent inflows into the business.

headline: Chris Andrews supports regulatory scrutiny of private credit sector as appropriate given influx of new managers, while cautioning investors to focus on asset quality, liquidity frameworks and manager track record over labels
reasoning: Andrews notes that the private credit space has seen a wave of new managers entering to capture investor demand, with most being quality operators but some substandard ones also entering the market. He believes regulatory scrutiny is well placed and ultimately beneficial to investors and the economy. Rather than focusing on whether a strategy is labelled 'private credit' or 'alternatives', he urges investors to assess three fundamentals: quality of the asset, liquidity management frameworks, and manager expertise with a track record of transparency and performance through the cycle.
quote: So we've seen this over many decades. Andrew, from time to time, particular segments of the market have a whole wash of new managers coming in. They identifying opportunities there, identifying investor demand, and they come in looking to fulfill that. Now very often those businesses are really good quality businesses. Sometimes though, you know, you do sometimes get some substandard operators in there as well. So in terms of regulatory focus, it's absolutely appropriate that all of these sort of new managers, the new approaches to to investment that are coming into the industry, get proper regulatory scrutiny. So I think that's important and ultimately to the benefit of investors and to the benefit of Australia's economy.

headline: Federal budget CGT changes are a modest tailwind for income-based investments relative to capital growth assets, but fundamentals should remain the primary investment driver
reasoning: Andrews acknowledges that the federal government's changes to capital gains tax treatment have made income-based returns relatively more attractive compared to capital-based returns on a post-budget basis. He frames this as a tailwind for La Trobe's business rather than a primary driver for investors. He cautions investors against making decisions based solely on tax considerations, instead emphasising asset quality, liquidity management frameworks, and manager track record as the three key criteria.
quote: That is a bit of a tailwind for our business. It's true Andrew, in the sense that these income based returns are continuing to grow on a relative basis in attractiveness to to capital based returns post the federal budget. But again, for investors, don't focus. You know, if you're making an investment decision based solely on tax, you're not making the right investment decision. Go back to the fundamentals. headline: Chris Andrews (La Trobe Financial) sees potential upward pressure on RBA rates amid inflation and productivity stagnation concerns, but remains broadly optimistic on Australia's economic resilience
reasoning: Andrews believes there is real pressure on inflation in Australia and expects the Reserve Bank may need to make an upward move on interest rates in coming months. He also flags ongoing challenges around stagnation of productivity growth as a structural concern. Despite these headwinds, he emphasises Australia's historical resilience across economic cycles and calls for measured, disciplined effort rather than alarm. He does not see it as 'emergency stations' but rather a time for focused competitive effort.
quote: It's a complex time for Australia. And Andrew and you know we're talking about there is real pressure on inflation. I think there's going to be pressure on the reserve Bank over the next few months to make an upward move in interest rates. Um, we certainly continue to have that challenge around the stagnation of productivity growth. And that's something as a nation that we simply cannot keep tolerating. But I would say this too. There's reasons for optimism. Australia as an economy has proven itself over very many decades to be extraordinarily resistant to the complexity of the economic cycle.
